group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 34-year-old woman was escorted to the emergency department near noon after waking with a sudden, deep right-sided chest ache that intensified whenever she coughed or tried to take a full breath; the cough had begun two days earlier as a dry throat tickle during her overnight shift in a data-processing office but by this morning carried a scant amount of blood-streaked sputum. Co-workers noted she looked flushed and was walking more slowly than usual, so they arranged ride-share transport rather than calling emergency medical services so that no treatments would be started en route. She reports feeling “thirsty all the time” since yesterday, attributing it to long hours at her desk and forgetting her water bottle; she measured her temperature at home with an infrared forehead scanner and found it to be 98.6 °F. There was no dizziness or light-headedness, and she denies confusion, focal weakness, or problems finding words. Five years ago she experienced a small left parietal ischemic event thought to be related to an oral contraceptive, leaving only a barely perceptible right-hand clumsiness when writing quickly; she takes no antiplatelet medication at present because follow-up imaging showed complete recanalization and her neurologist cleared her after six months of dual therapy at that time. Three years ago she was diagnosed with autoimmune hepatitis after persistently elevated transaminases; a liver biopsy demonstrated early interface activity without bridging fibrosis, and she has remained on azathioprine 50 mg nightly with monthly blood monitoring. She has never been told she has chronic kidney trouble, cardiomyopathy, or pulmonary disease, and her most recent outpatient basic metabolic panel four months earlier was completely normal. She does not smoke, drinks a glass of wine on special occasions only, and denies recreational drug use. Vaccination records on the state registry confirm receipt of last season’s influenza shot and a single dose of conjugate pneumococcal vaccine two years ago given by her primary-care clinician. She took no antibiotics, steroids, antipyretics, nebulized medications, or supplemental oxygen prior to arrival. On initial evaluation, before any intravenous lines were flushed with saline, she was sitting upright on the stretcher, speaking in full sentences, and correctly stated the date, location, and current national holiday; pupils were briskly reactive and extra-ocular movements intact. Her skin appeared dry and slightly sunburned from a recent weekend hike, capillary refill was less than two seconds, and mucous membranes were tacky. Triage vitals obtained on room air at an altitude of 180 m showed oral temperature 98.6 °F, regular but rapid radial pulse 128 beats per minute, non-invasive blood pressure 94/52 mm Hg confirmed manually, respiratory rate 56 breaths per minute with shallow excursions and faint intercostal retractions, and fingertip pulse oximetry oscillating between 96 % and 97 %. Neck veins were not distended, and there was no peripheral edema. Cardiac auscultation revealed a fast, crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs transmitted diminished breath sounds with coarse late-inspiratory crackles over the right middle and lower posterior zones; percussion remained resonant throughout, and there was no egophony or dull stony note to suggest free pleural fluid. The abdominal exam showed a soft contour; a smooth liver edge was palpable 1 cm below the costal margin but nontender, and there was no splenomegaly or shifting dullness. Strength was 5/5 in all major muscle groups, finger-to-nose testing was steady, and reflexes were symmetric. Bedside capillary glucose measured 111 mg/dL. Within ten minutes of arrival, venous blood drawn before any intravenous fluids revealed sodium 163 mEq/L, potassium 3.9 mEq/L, chloride 118 mEq/L, bicarbonate 18 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 59 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, and hematocrit 64 %. A right radial arterial sample on ambient air returned pH 7.19, PaCO₂ 32 mm Hg, PaO₂ 99 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, consistent with a primary metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory compensation. White blood cell count was 15.2 × 10⁹/L with 87 % neutrophils and no bandemia; platelet count was 235 × 10⁹/L. High-sensitivity troponin was undetectable, and serum lactate measured 1.6 mmol/L. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph taken before any medications demonstrated a patchy consolidation occupying the posterior segment of the right upper lobe and superior portion of the right lower lobe with air bronchograms; both costophrenic angles remained sharp, and no meniscus or layering opacity was seen. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia at 126 beats per minute with normal intervals and no acute ischemic changes. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, an induced sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigen testing for common bacterial pathogens, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched prior to the ordering of antibiotics or intravenous crystalloid. Up to the moment this narrative is logged, she has not received fluids, vasopressors, antipyretics, bronchodilators, or supplemental oxygen, thereby preserving all physiologic observations, laboratory values, and imaging findings as her untreated state on presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and imaging points at presentation.
- Demographics: a 34-year-old woman starts at age minus 10 = 24. No nursing-home residence → 0.
- Comorbidities: chronic liver disease (autoimmune hepatitis) → 20; cerebrovascular disease (prior ischemic stroke) → 10. No malignancy, heart failure, or chronic renal disease → 0 each.
- Examination: respiratory rate 56/min (≥30) → 20; pulse 128/min (≥125) → 10. Mentation is normal, systolic BP 94 mmHg is not <90, and temperature 37°C is neither <35 nor ≥40 → 0 each.
- Tests: arterial pH 7.19 (<7.35) → 30; BUN 59 mg/dL (≥30) → 20. Sodium 163 is not <130 mEq/L, glucose 111 is not ≥250 mg/dL, hematocrit 64% is not <30%, and room-air PaO₂ 99 is not <60 mmHg → 0 each. No pleural effusion → 0.
Sum: 24 + 20 + 10 + 20 + 10 + 30 + 20 = 134 (risk class V).
Final answer: 134
